name: Reactor
intent: Wait for events from many sources in one place, and dispatch each ready event to the handler that deals with it.
scenario: A chat server has thousands of open connections. Most are quiet, and a few send a message at any moment.
problem: The server gives each connection its own thread, which blocks on reading. Thousands of mostly idle threads cost memory and scheduling time, and the program spends its effort on waiting rather than on work.
solution: A Reactor owns a loop. Connections are registered with it, each with a handler. The loop asks the operating system's event demultiplexer (select, epoll, kqueue) which connections are ready, and calls the handler for each one. A handler does its small piece of work without blocking and returns, so one thread serves all connections. Servers often run one reactor loop per core, and give slow or heavy work to a separate pool of workers.
pain: One thread per connection, and nearly all of them are asleep
Memory and scheduling cost grow with the number of connections
Many threads sharing state need many locks
The server cannot hold many more connections than it has threads to spare
benefits: One thread can serve thousands of connections
Handlers on one loop run one at a time, so data used only by that loop needs no locks
Cost grows with activity, not with the number of idle connections
The handling of each kind of event is separated into its own handler
whenToUse: Many connections or sources, most of them idle at any moment
Work per event is short and mostly waits for input and output
You want to avoid the cost and locking of many threads
whenNotToUse: A few connections with heavy work each: threads or processes use the cores better
Handlers that must block, such as with a blocking database driver
CPU-bound work: one loop runs on one core, so it needs a worker pool beside it
pitfalls: A handler that blocks or computes for a long time holds up every other connection on its loop
Code written in a callback style spreads one task over several handlers and is harder to follow
One loop uses one core: scale with a loop per core, or workers for CPU-heavy work
An unhandled error in a handler can stop the whole loop if it is not caught

roles.label: Event source
roles.description: A connection or file that becomes ready to read or write.

roles.label: Event demultiplexer
roles.description: The operating system call (select, epoll, kqueue) that reports which sources are ready.

roles.label: Reactor
roles.description: Owns the loop: waits on the demultiplexer, and dispatches each ready event to its handler.

roles.label: Event handler
roles.description: Code that deals with one kind of event. It must be quick and must not block.

quiz.question: A chat server uses one thread per connection. At 20,000 mostly idle connections it runs out of memory and spends its time switching between threads. What is the best change?
options: Buy a server with more memory, and raise the limit on the number of threads
Serve connections with a reactor loop that uses non-blocking I/O and the operating system's event notification
Close each connection after every message, and make clients reconnect when they have more to say
Make each thread's stack smaller so that more of them fit in the same amount of memory
quiz.explanation: Idle connections cost almost nothing in a reactor, which only works on those that are ready. More memory and smaller stacks only raise the ceiling, and reconnecting for every message adds heavy handshake work.

quiz.question: A reactor-based server answers quickly, but every few seconds all clients see a pause of about 200 ms. The profiler shows one handler making a blocking database call. What is the best fix?
options: Add more connections to the loop, so that the pauses are spread more evenly
Make the reactor wait a little longer between loops, so that the handler has time to finish
Let the other handlers skip the loop while that one handler is running its query
Use a non-blocking database call, or hand the query to a worker pool and reply when it returns
quiz.explanation: The loop can only run one handler at a time, so a blocking handler stalls everyone. Keep handlers short by using non-blocking calls or by moving the slow work elsewhere. The other options do not remove the blocked loop.

quiz.question: A handler resizes images on the reactor loop. Other clients wait while it works, and the server's other cores are idle. What is the best design?
options: Move the CPU-heavy work to a worker pool, and run one reactor loop per core
Make the image resize run twice as fast by using a more efficient library inside the handler
Run the resize in the handler, but only when no other client has a message waiting
Replace the reactor with one thread per client, because reactors cannot handle heavy work
quiz.explanation: A reactor is for waiting on many sources, so heavy computation belongs in workers, and more loops use more cores. A faster library only shortens the stall, and the scheduling idea is not possible, since events arrive at any time. Threads per client give up the reactor's advantages for all handlers.
